chunks.text: The Royal Inscriptions of Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar II, and Their Successors

The so-called “Neo-Babylonian Dynasty” was founded by  Nabopolassar II  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/babylon7/rulers/nabopolassar/index.html] , a self-proclaimed “son of nobody” who brought the once-great Assyrian empire to an end. Under the five kings who reigned after him, especially his son and immediate successor, the famous  Nebuchadnezzar II  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/babylon7/rulers/nebuchadnezzarii/index.html] , Babylon regained its former glory and made a deep, lasting impression, one that still persists today. Numerous officially commissioned records of the deeds of  Nabopolassar II  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/babylon7/rulers/nabopolassar/index.html] ,  Nebuchadnezzar II  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/babylon7/rulers/nebuchadnezzarii/index.html] , and their successors, in particular the dynasty’s sixth and last ruler  Nabonidus II  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/babylon7/rulers/nabonidus/index.html] , were unearthed at the very beginning of the twentieth century, when a German team of archaeologists led by Robert Koldewey excavated sections of the legendary ancient city of Babylon, the fame of whose temple-tower and “hanging gardens” were well-known from the Bible and Classical sources. This website presents some of the royal inscriptions of the six kings of Babylon who ruled modern-day southern Iraq from 625 BC to 539 BC, together with a few resources and materials for their study and their historical context.      RIBo, a sub-project of the Official Inscriptions of the Middle East in Antiquity (OIMEA) Project, publishes editions of Akkadian and Sumerian inscriptions from Babylonia in the late second and first millennia BC. The corpus of edited texts in this RIBo sub-project (“Babylon 7”) presently includes:

This open-access sub-project of the  Royal Inscriptions of Babylonia online (RIBo) Project  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/]  is intended to present up-to-date editions of the officially commissioned texts of the six kings of the Neo-Babylonian Dynasty (625-539 BC). “Babylon 7,” or “The Royal Inscriptions of Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar II, and Their Successors,” carries on where the now defunct RIMB (Royal Inscriptions of Mesopotamia, Babylonian Periods) publications of the Toronto-based Royal Inscriptions of Mesopotamia (RIM) Project ended.     Numerous inscriptions of the dynasty’s most famous kings (Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar II, and Nabonidus), as well as a few from the reigns of its lesser known rulers (Amēl-Marduk, Neriglissar, and Lābaši-Marduk), have been published. Many inscribed objects of theirs were unearthed at the beginning of the twentieth century when German archaeologists excavated Babylon (1899–1917). Although Rocío Da Riva has made available transliterations and translations of the official texts of Nabopolassar, Amēl-Marduk, and Neriglissar (2013), as well as a few of the more important inscriptions of Nebuchadnezzar II (2012), and Hanspeter Schaudig has published editions of Nabonidus’ inscriptions (2001), no comprehensive publication of editions of the complete corpus of royal inscriptions of the Neo-Babylonian Dynasty has appeared. Such an undertaking has been in the works since 1979, when A. Kirk Grayson initiated the RIM Project at the University of Toronto; these texts were to be edited as volumes 3 and 4 of the RIMB sub-series. It is planned, in cooperation with Grant Frame (director of the  Royal Inscriptions of the Neo-Assyrian Period [RINAP] Project  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/rinap/] ), that this LMU-based open-access project brings together in a single place transliterations and English translations of all of the royal inscriptions of Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar II, and their successors, as well as creates explanatory and supplementary materials in order to provide some historical context for the texts.           Sponsors and timing       This website was created as part of the research project Official Inscriptions of the Middle East in Antiquity (OIMEA), whose funding is provided by the  Alexander von Humboldt Foundation  [https://www.humboldt-foundation.de/web/home.html]  (through the establishment of the  Alexander von Humboldt Chair for Ancient History of the Near and Middle East  [http://www.ag.geschichte.uni-muenchen.de/lehrstuehle/ls_radner/index.html] ) and  Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München  [http://www.uni-muenchen.de/index.html]  ( Historisches Seminar  [http://www.geschichte.uni-muenchen.de/index.html]  -  Abteilung Alte Geschichte  [http://www.ag.geschichte.uni-muenchen.de/index.html] ). The project began in late 2015 and Phase 1 of the website was made available in early 2016. The “Babylon 7” sub-project of  RIBo  [http://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/ribo/]  is intended to be a long term endeavor since there is much work to do and finish before we have reached our primary objects. Please bear with us as we expand, improve, and refine our content.
